title: Designing ML Systems: Interview Notes

Designing ML Systems: Interview Notes

Personal notes on Chip Huyen’s Designing Machine Learning Systems (O’Reilly, First Edition, 2022), written to prepare for machine learning interviews. title: Chapter 1: Overview of Machine Learning Systems
text:
What an ML system is
Overview. This chapter asks two questions before any model is trained: when is machine learning (ML) the right tool at all, and what changes when a model leaves the notebook and runs in production? The answers set up the rest of the book. A production ML system is mostly not the algorithm. It is the requirements, data, infrastructure, and the logic for deploying, monitoring, and updating models. Most of the chapter contrasts ML in research with ML in production along five axes (stakeholders, computational priority, data, fairness, interpretability), then contrasts ML systems with traditional software.
When people hear “machine learning system,” they usually picture the algorithm: logistic regression, a gradient-boosted tree, a neural network. What else has to exist before that algorithm is useful to anyone?
The book is organized around this picture. Figure 1 redraws the book’s Figure 1-1 and marks which chapter covers each part.
Two terms come up immediately and are easy to blur in an interview.
So MLOps names the practices and tooling, and systems design is the discipline of fitting all the pieces (and people) together. The book deliberately covers no algorithm in detail. Algorithms go out of date quickly, while the framework for choosing and running one should survive them.

title: Chapter 1: Overview of Machine Learning Systems
text:
When to use machine learning
ML can solve many problems, but even for problems it can solve, it may not be the best solution. Before starting a project, ask whether ML is necessary and whether it is cost-effective. (The book notes it never asks whether ML is sufficient, because the answer is always no: ML is always one part of a larger system.)

The five-part test
The book frames what ML does in one sentence and then examines each part.

Definition. Machine learning is an approach to (1) learn (2) complex patterns from (3) existing data and use these patterns to make (4) predictions on (5) unseen data.

Each phrase is a condition a problem must satisfy.

Learn: the system can learn. A relational database is not an ML system. You can state a relationship between two columns, but the database cannot discover one. In supervised learning, the system learns from input–output pairs. The book’s running example: learn to predict an Airbnb listing’s rental price from its characteristics (square footage, rooms, neighborhood, amenities, rating), given a dataset of listings and their prices.
Complex patterns: there are patterns, and they are complex. There is no pattern to learn in the outcome of a fair die. (The book separates patterns from distributions: we know the distribution of a fair die exactly, but nothing about how each outcome is generated is learnable.) If the pattern is simple, skip ML. Mapping an Airbnb listing’s zip code to its state needs a lookup table, not a model. Mapping a listing’s characteristics to its price is complex enough that hand-specifying it is impractical, which is where ML fits. What is complex for machines differs from what is complex for humans: raising a number to the power of 10 is easy for a machine, while spotting a cat in a photo used to be hard.
Existing data: data is available, or can be collected. No tax and income records, no tax-prediction model. Two edge cases look like exceptions but are not. In zero-shot learning, a model predicts well on a task it never saw data for, but it was trained on data for related tasks. In continual learning, a model can be deployed untrained and learn from production traffic, at the risk of a poor experience for early users. Without data, some companies “fake it till they make it”: humans make the predictions at first, and the logged results later become training data.
Predictions: the problem is predictive. ML outputs predictions, so it suits problems where many cheap, approximate answers are useful. Many questions can be reframed as “what would the answer be?”, including about the present or past. Compute-heavy processes are a common case: rather than run the exact computation, train a model to approximate its output (the book’s examples are image denoising and screen-space shading in graphics).
Unseen data: unseen data shares patterns with the training data. A model trained on 2008 app-store data will not predict which apps get downloaded on Christmas 2020. Technically, training and unseen data should come from similar distributions. We cannot know the distribution of data we have not seen, so we assume (for instance, that users behave tomorrow roughly as they did today) and check with monitoring.


Definition. Condition 5 is the informal version of the assumption that data are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.): training examples and future examples are drawn from the same distribution. When that fails in production we call it distribution shift.

Distribution shift is the subject of Chapter 8 (monitoring), and adapting to it is Chapter 9 (continual learning and testing in production).
Figure 2 shows the contrast behind conditions 1 and 2. Traditional software takes inputs plus hand-written patterns and produces outputs. ML takes inputs plus outputs and produces the patterns. This is why Andrej Karpathy called ML “Software 2.0.”

Figure 2. Traditional software needs the pattern specified by hand. ML learns the pattern from input–output examples (after the book's Figure 1-2).



When ML shines
Given how most current algorithms learn, ML works especially well when the problem has four more traits.

It is repetitive. Humans learn from a few examples. Most ML algorithms need many, so a pattern that repeats often is easier to learn.
Wrong predictions are cheap. No model is right every time. Recommender systems are a large ML use case partly because a bad recommendation costs little: the user just does not click. If a single mistake can be catastrophic, ML can still make sense when the benefit of correct predictions outweighs the cost of wrong ones on average. The book’s example is self-driving cars, which are worth pursuing if they become statistically safer than human drivers despite the risk of fatal errors.
It is at scale. ML needs real up-front investment in data, compute, infrastructure, and people, so it pays off when the model makes many predictions. Some problems that look like one prediction are really many. An election-outcome model predicts once every four years in name, but in practice it updates its prediction hourly as new information arrives. Scale also means more data to train on.
The patterns keep changing. Hand-written rules go stale. Spam that today features a foreign prince will tomorrow feature something else. An ML model can be retrained on new data without anyone working out exactly how the data changed (this is the problem concept drift names; Chapters 8 and 9 return to it).

The “wrong predictions are cheap” trait is an expected value argument. Written as a rule of thumb:


P(\text{correct}) \cdot \text{benefit} \;>\; P(\text{wrong}) \cdot \text{cost}


The left side is the average value of being right and the right side is the average cost of being wrong. ML is a reasonable choice when the expected value of acting on its predictions beats the expected cost of its errors, even if individual errors are severe.


When not to use ML
Most current ML algorithms should not be used if any of these hold:

It is unethical. (The book’s Chapter 11 has a case study on an automated grader’s biases.)
A simpler solution does the job. Chapter 6 makes “start with a non-ML solution” the first phase of model development.
It is not cost-effective.

Even when ML cannot solve a whole problem, it may solve a piece of it. If a chatbot cannot answer every customer query, a model can still predict whether a query matches a frequently asked question: if so, show the answer; if not, route the customer to a human. The book also cautions against rejecting a technology only because it is not cost-effective yet, since most advances are incremental and waiting for others to prove it can leave a company years behind.

title: Chapter 1: Overview of Machine Learning Systems
text:
Machine learning use cases
Consumers meet ML mainly through search and recommendations, predictive typing, photo enhancement, face or fingerprint unlock, machine translation, smart assistants, and home monitoring (such as fall detection for an elderly person living alone). But most ML use cases are in the enterprise, and enterprise requirements differ.

Definition. As a general tendency (with many exceptions), enterprise ML applications have stricter accuracy requirements but are more forgiving of latency than consumer applications.

The book’s reasoning: moving a speech recognizer from 95% to 95.5% accuracy is unnoticeable to most consumers, but a 0.1% efficiency gain in a large company’s resource allocation can be worth millions. Meanwhile, a one-second delay can send a consumer to another app, while an enterprise user will usually wait.
The enterprise uses the chapter names, grouped by what they do:



Use case
What the model predicts




Fraud detection
Whether a transaction is fraudulent, learned from past fraud (anomaly detection); one of the oldest enterprise uses


Price optimization
The price for a time period that maximizes an objective (margin, revenue, growth); suits many transactions with fluctuating demand, such as ads, flights, ride-sharing


Demand forecasting
Customer demand, for budgeting, inventory, and staffing (understock loses sales; overstock spoils)


Customer acquisition
Which prospects to target, which ads to show, when to offer discounts


Churn prediction
When a customer (or employee) is about to leave (customer attrition); retaining a customer is estimated to cost 5 to 25 times less than acquiring a new one


Support ticket classification
Which department a ticket should go to, shortening response time


Brand monitoring
Mentions of the brand and their sentiment (sentiment analysis)



Health care is singled out. There are systems that detect skin cancer and diagnose diabetes, but because of strict accuracy and privacy requirements they are usually delivered through a health-care provider or used to assist a clinician’s diagnosis, rather than sold directly to consumers.

section: ML in research versus in production
text:
ML in research versus in production
Most people with ML expertise learned it in academia: courses, research, papers. The book’s claim is that production ML differs from research ML in at least five ways, summarized in its Table 1-1.



Table 2.1: Key differences between ML in research and in production (after the book’s Table 1-1).











Research
Production




Requirements
State-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets
Different stakeholders have different requirements


Computational priority
Fast training, high throughput
Fast inference, low latency


Data
Static
Constantly shifting


Fairness
Often not a focus
Must be considered


Interpretability
Often not a focus
Must be considered







Stakeholders and requirements
A research or leaderboard project usually has one objective: beat the state of the art on a benchmark. A production project has many stakeholders, each with their own, often conflicting, requirements.
The book’s running example is a restaurant-recommendation app that earns a 10% service fee on each order, so expensive orders earn more.

ML engineers want to recommend the restaurants users are most likely to order from, and believe a more complex model with more data will do it.
Sales wants to recommend expensive restaurants, because they bring in larger fees.
Product has seen that every increase in latency loses orders, and wants recommendations returned in under 100 milliseconds.
The ML platform team is being paged at night over scaling problems, and wants to pause model updates to fix the platform.
The manager wants to maximize margin (and one way to do that might be to cut the ML team).

“Recommend what users will most likely click” and “recommend what earns the most” are different objectives. Chapter 2 resolves this by decoupling objectives: train one model per objective and combine their predictions. Suppose model A optimizes clicks and model B optimizes revenue, and neither meets the 100 ms requirement. Which do we deploy? It depends on how strict each requirement is. If 100 ms is a must-have (say, the company found 10% of users close the app beyond that), neither model works. If it is a nice-to-have, either might. Part of the ML engineer’s job is finding out which requirements are hard constraints.
This mismatch is one reason successful research often does not ship. Ensemble learning is the book’s example.

Definition. Ensembling combines multiple learning algorithms to obtain better predictive performance than any of the constituent algorithms could alone.

Ensembles win competitions, including the Netflix Prize, but they are not widely used in production. The small accuracy gain usually costs slower predictions and results that are harder to interpret. (Chapter 6 covers ensembles properly.) Whether a small gain is worth that cost depends on the task. A 0.2% improvement in click-through rate for an e-commerce recommender can be worth millions in revenue. For many other tasks users would not notice a small gain, so a complex model has to beat a simple one by a wide margin to justify itself.






Note



Criticism of ML leaderboards. The book summarizes three objections to leaderboards like Kaggle, ImageNet, and GLUE:

The hard steps of building an ML system (framing the problem, collecting and labeling data) are already done for you.
When many teams evaluate against the same held-out test set, one model can come out on top by chance. This is a multiple comparisons problem.
Ethayarajh and Jurafsky (EMNLP 2020) argue that benchmarks reward accuracy at the expense of qualities practitioners value, such as compactness, fairness, and energy efficiency.





Computational priorities
People who have not deployed a model tend to focus on model development and neglect deployment and maintenance. During development we train many models, each over many passes through the training data, and evaluate each once on a smaller validation set, so training is the bottleneck. Once deployed, the model’s job is to make predictions, so inference is the bottleneck. Research prioritizes fast training; production prioritizes fast inference.
A corollary is that research cares about throughput and production cares about latency.

Definition. Latency is the time from receiving a query to returning its result. Throughput is how many queries are processed in a given period of time.

The book flags a terminology clash. Kleppmann’s Designing Data-Intensive Applications separates response time (what the client sees, including network and queueing delays) from latency (only the time a request waits to be handled). The book, following ML usage, uses “latency” to mean the full response time: from when a request is sent to when the response arrives. In an interview it is worth saying which one you mean.

Latency and throughput under batching
If a system handles one query at a time, the two quantities are tied: higher latency means lower throughput. At 10 ms per query, throughput is 100 queries per second; at 100 ms, it is 10. Most modern systems instead process queries in batches, often concurrently, and then higher latency can come with higher throughput. When batches run one after another,


\text{throughput} = \frac{\text{batch size}}{\text{time per batch}}


so a larger batch can raise throughput even if each batch takes longer.






Note



Worked example (the book’s numbers).

One query at a time, 10 ms each: latency 10 ms, throughput 1 / 0.010\,\text{s} = 100 queries/s.
Batches of 10, each taking 10 ms: latency is still 10 ms, but throughput is 10 / 0.010\,\text{s} = 1{,}000 queries/s.
Batches of 50, each taking 20 ms: latency rises to 20 ms, and throughput rises to 50 / 0.020\,\text{s} = 2{,}500 queries/s.

In the last line both latency and throughput went up compared with the first.

Figure 3. Over the same 40 ms window: one query per run trades latency against throughput, while batching can raise both (after the book's Figure 1-4).

These numbers leave out one cost. For online queries, a batch has to fill before it runs, so each query also waits for the others to arrive, which adds latency the worked example does not count. Research happily trades latency for throughput through aggressive batching. Production often cannot: lowering latency may mean running fewer queries at a time on the same hardware, which underuses that hardware and raises the cost per query.
Latency matters commercially. The book cites a 2017 Akamai study finding that a 100 ms delay can cut conversion rates by 7%, and Booking.com finding that roughly 30% more latency cost about 0.5% in conversions.


Latency is a distribution
It is tempting to summarize latency as one number, the mean over a time window. That number can mislead, because latency is a distribution and the mean is pulled by outliers.

Definition. The q-th percentile (written pq) of a set of measurements is a value below which roughly q% of the measurements fall. p50 is the median: half of requests are faster, half slower. Latency targets usually use high percentiles: p90, p95, p99 (sometimes p99.9).







Note



Worked example (the book’s 10 requests). Latencies in ms: 100, 102, 100, 100, 99, 104, 110, 90, 3,000, 95.

Mean. The sum is 3,900 ms, so the mean is 3{,}900 / 10 = 390 ms. Nine of ten requests took about 100 ms, so 390 ms makes the system look much slower than it usually is.
Sort. 90, 95, 99, 100, 100, 100, 102, 104, 110, 3,000.
Median (p50). The middle two values are 100 and 100, so p50 = 100 ms, which describes the typical request.
The outlier. The 3,000 ms request is an outlier, perhaps a network error, and is worth investigating on its own.



The book says the p90 of these ten requests is 3,000 ms. That depends on which percentile definition you use, and with only ten samples the definitions disagree widely:

Nearest rank (take the \lceil 0.9 \times 10 \rceil = 9th sorted value): p90 = 110 ms.
Linear interpolation (NumPy’s default; position 0.9 \times (10-1) = 8.1 in 0-indexed order, so one tenth of the way from 110 to 3,000): p90 = 110 + 0.1 \times 2{,}890 = 399 ms.
Round up to the next sample (NumPy’s method="higher"): p90 = 3,000 ms, the book’s figure.

The practical lesson is that a tail percentile computed from a handful of requests is unstable. A real p99 needs enough traffic that 1% of it is many requests.
High percentiles matter because the slowest requests can come from the most important users. At Amazon, the customers with the slowest requests are often those with the most data on their accounts, because they have made the most purchases. So performance requirements are commonly written as tail percentiles, for example “p90 (or p99.9) latency must stay below some threshold.”



Data
Research datasets are clean, well formatted, and static so the community can benchmark against them. Many people have used them, their quirks are known, and preprocessing scripts are often public.
Production data, if it exists at all, is messier:

noisy, possibly unstructured, and constantly shifting;
likely biased, in ways you probably do not know;
labels, if any, may be sparse, imbalanced, or wrong, and changing business requirements can force relabeling;
user data brings privacy and regulatory obligations.

Research mostly uses historical data that already sits somewhere. Production also consumes data generated continuously by users, systems, and third parties. The book illustrates this with a graphic adapted from Andrej Karpathy (its Figure 1-5): during his PhD most of his time went to models and little to data, while at Tesla the proportions reversed.


Fairness
In research a model is not yet used on people, so fairness is easy to postpone: “get state of the art first, worry about fairness in production.” By production it is too late. Accuracy and latency have public benchmarks to beat; fairness, as of the book’s writing, has no equivalent state of the art.
The examples are concrete: a loan rejected because the model leans on zip code, which encodes socioeconomic background; a résumé ranked lower because of the spelling of a name; a mortgage rate tied to credit scores that favor the wealthy. The book quotes a 2019 Berkeley study finding that lenders rejected about 1.3 million creditworthy Black and Latino applicants between 2008 and 2015.

Definition. Algorithmic bias is systematic error in a model’s outputs that disadvantages some group. In the book’s phrasing, ML algorithms “don’t predict the future, but encode the past,” so they reproduce the biases in their training data, and at scale.

Scale is what makes this worse than individual human bias. A human makes sweeping judgments about a few people at a time; a model can make them about millions in seconds. And aggregate metrics hide it. Errors on a minority group barely move overall performance: a model that is correct on 98% of a population can be badly wrong on the other 2%, and if fixing that 2% would cost several times more, some companies choose not to. This is the same arithmetic as a rare-positive classification problem, where a high overall accuracy says little about the small class. Chapter 11 covers fairness and responsible AI in depth.


Interpretability
Geoffrey Hinton posed this question in 2020: if you had cancer, would you choose a black-box AI surgeon with a 90% cure rate that cannot explain how it works, or a human surgeon with an 80% cure rate? When the book’s author asked 30 technology executives, they split about evenly.

Definition. A model is interpretable (or explainable; see explainable artificial intelligence) to the extent that people can understand why it produced a given output.

Research is still scored mainly on performance, so researchers have little incentive to work on interpretability. In industry it is usually a requirement, for two reasons:

For users (business leaders and end users): to understand why a decision was made, so they can trust the model and detect the biases described above.
For developers: to debug and improve the model.

In some countries and for some uses there is also a legal right to explanation of an algorithm’s output. This is the clinical setting of the Hinton question: a clinician deciding whether to act on a model’s flag needs a reason, not only a score. The book does not cover specific explanation methods in this chapter.
The book closes the comparison with a short discussion: knowing only the academic side of ML is fine, but most companies cannot fund pure research without short-term applications, so most ML jobs are, and will be, in putting ML into production.

title: Chapter 1: Overview of Machine Learning Systems
text:
ML systems versus traditional software
ML is part of software engineering, and software engineering has decades of production practice. Why not just apply those practices? Partly we should: production ML would be better if ML practitioners were better software engineers, and many standard tools apply. But some challenges are specific to ML.
Code and data are entangled. Software engineering separates concerns and keeps code and data apart (separation of concerns). An ML system is part code, part data, and part artifacts built from both. Because the best data tends to win, companies put more effort into data than into algorithms, and because data changes quickly, ML systems need faster development and deployment cycles.
Data must be tested and versioned too. In ordinary software we test and version code. In ML we also have to test and version data, which is harder. How do you version a large dataset? How do you tell whether a sample helps or hurts?
Not all samples are equally valuable. The book’s example: a model already trained on one million scans of normal lungs and one thousand scans of cancerous lungs gains far more from another cancerous scan than another normal one. This is the class-imbalance problem seen from the data side, and Chapter 4 (training data) returns to it. Accepting all incoming data indiscriminately can hurt performance and expose the model to data poisoning, where an attacker plants training examples to manipulate the model (a form of adversarial machine learning).
Models are large. As of 2022, models with hundreds of millions or billions of parameters need gigabytes of memory just to load. Getting them into production, especially on edge devices (covered in Chapter 7), is a major engineering task, and they also have to run fast enough to be useful. An autocomplete model that is slower than your typing is useless. The book’s example of progress: in 2018 people called BERT (large BERT: 340 million parameters, 1.35 GB) too big and slow to be practical; two years later it and its variants were used in almost every English search on Google.
Monitoring and debugging are harder. As models grow more complex and less transparent, it is harder to see what went wrong, or to be alerted quickly when something does.

title: Chapter 1: Overview of Machine Learning Systems
text:
Summary






Note



Key takeaways from Chapter 1 (and what an interviewer is usually checking):

The algorithm is a small part of the system. Requirements, data, infrastructure, and deployment, monitoring, and update logic are most of the work. MLOps is the tooling and practice; ML systems design is fitting the whole thing together.
Justify ML before using it. Check the five-part test (learn, complex patterns, existing data, predictive, unseen data resembles training data) and the four traits (repetitive, cheap errors on average, at scale, changing patterns). Name the alternatives: a lookup table, a rule, or a non-ML baseline.
Production has many stakeholders. Expect conflicting objectives, and separate must-have constraints from nice-to-haves. Ensembles show how a research win can fail production constraints on latency and interpretability.
Latency and throughput are different. Batching can raise both. Production usually optimizes latency, and latency should be reported as percentiles (p50, p90, p99), not a mean, with enough samples for the tail to be stable.
Production data shifts. Training and serving distributions should match (the i.i.d. assumption), and in production they often drift.
Fairness and interpretability are requirements in production. Aggregate accuracy can hide failure on a small subgroup; users need explanations to trust a model, and developers need them to debug it.
ML differs from traditional software because data is part of the system: it needs testing and versioning, samples differ in value, and it can be poisoned.



Next chapter: Chapter 2, Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design, connects business objectives to ML objectives, sets out the requirements for an ML system (reliability, scalability, maintainability, adaptability), describes the iterative development process, and covers framing ML problems, including choosing objective functions and decoupling objectives.

title: Chapter 1 practice: Overview of Machine Learning Systems
text:
Problem 1: Does this task need ML at all?
Overview. These are interview-style questions on Chapter 1. Answer each one out loud before opening the worked solution, the way you would in an interview. The scenarios and numbers are invented for practice. Each solution says which chapter section it draws on, walks through the reasoning, and ends with a short answer you could give.
A hospital IT lead says: “We want to use AI for three things: (a) mapping drug brand names to their generic names, (b) predicting which discharged patients will be readmitted within 30 days, and (c) flagging duplicate patient records where the same person was registered twice with small spelling differences.” Which of these would you use ML for, and why?
crumbs: 3  Chapter 1 practice: Overview of Machine Learning Systems

title: Chapter 1 practice: Overview of Machine Learning Systems
text:
TipWorked solution





This uses Chapter 1, The five-part test and When not to use ML.
The test is whether there is a complex pattern to learn from existing data, and whether a simpler solution would already work.

(a) Brand to generic name. The relationship is fixed and known: each brand maps to a defined generic. Like the book’s zip-code-to-state example, this is a lookup table maintained from a drug reference database. ML would add error to a problem that has an exact answer.
(b) 30-day readmission. Readmission depends on many interacting factors (diagnoses, prior admissions, medications, follow-up care), and no one can write that rule down by hand. There is historical data with outcomes, the task is predictive, it repeats for every discharge, and it runs at scale. This fits ML, provided future patients resemble past ones.
(c) Duplicate records. This sits in between. Exact matching on identifiers is a rule, not ML. But spelling variants, transposed dates, and changed addresses form a messy pattern that hand-written rules handle badly, and labeled examples of confirmed duplicates often exist. A reasonable answer is to start with rules and add a learned matcher for the cases rules miss. This is the book’s point about using ML for part of a problem.

Answer: (a) no, use a lookup table; (b) yes; (c) rules first, and ML for the fuzzy matches the rules miss.

title: Chapter 1 practice: Overview of Machine Learning Systems
section: Problem 2: Predicting adverse reactions before there is trial data
text:
Problem 2: Predicting adverse reactions before there is trial data
A pharma team asks: “Can we build a model now to predict which patients will have an adverse reaction to our new drug? It hasn’t entered clinical trials yet.” Walk through whether ML can do this, condition by condition, and say what you would propose.






TipWorked solution





This uses Chapter 1, The five-part test.
Go through the five conditions:

Learn. Only if there is something to learn from.
Complex patterns. Plausibly yes: who reacts badly likely depends on genetics, other conditions, other medications, and dose in complicated ways.
Existing data. This is where it fails. There are no outcomes for this drug. Two partial workarounds from the chapter:

Zero-shot-style transfer. Train on adverse-event data from related drugs (the same class or mechanism) and apply it to the new drug. The model still learns from data, just not data for this exact task.
“Fake it till you make it.” Have experts make the risk judgments during early trials, and log their judgments and the outcomes as future training data.

Predictions. Yes, it is a predictive question.
Unseen data resembles training data. This is the main risk of the transfer approach. Patients on a new drug, and the drug’s biology, may differ from the related drugs the model learned from, so we are assuming the distributions are similar. That needs checking as soon as trial data arrives.

Also note the cost of errors. The chapter says ML suits problems where wrong predictions are cheap, or where the benefits outweigh the costs on average. Missing a serious reaction is expensive, so any early model should support expert judgment rather than replace it.
Answer: Not as a standalone model yet, because condition 3 fails. Propose transfer from related drugs plus expert review, collect outcomes during the trials, and retrain once real data exists, checking that the new patients resemble the training data.

title: Chapter 1 practice: Overview of Machine Learning Systems
text:
Problem 3: Batching, latency, and cost
A model serving team measures three ways to run the same model on one GPU:



Option
How queries are processed
Time per run




A
one query at a time
8 ms


B
batches of 32
16 ms per batch


C
batches of 128
40 ms per batch



The product requirement is that every response returns within 30 ms. Traffic is 3,200 queries per second, arriving into a single shared queue.

What is the throughput of each option on one GPU, and what is the processing latency?
Which options can meet 30 ms once you count the time a query waits for its batch to fill?
How many GPUs does each feasible option need to serve 3,200 queries per second?







TipWorked solution





This uses Chapter 1, Latency and throughput under batching.
1. Throughput and processing latency. Throughput is batch size divided by time per batch:

A: 1 / 0.008\,\text{s} = 125 queries/s, latency 8 ms.
B: 32 / 0.016\,\text{s} = 2{,}000 queries/s, latency 16 ms.
C: 128 / 0.040\,\text{s} = 3{,}200 queries/s, latency 40 ms.

Option C already misses 30 ms on processing time alone.
2. Add the batch-fill wait. The chapter warns that online batching makes queries wait for the batch to fill. At 3,200 queries per second, filling a batch takes:

B: 32 / 3{,}200 = 0.010\,\text{s} = 10 ms. The first query in a batch waits about 10 ms, then 16 ms of processing, so about 26 ms in the worst case. That is within 30 ms.
C: 128 / 3{,}200 = 40 ms of filling plus 40 ms of processing, about 80 ms. It fails.
A: no fill wait, 8 ms. It passes.

3. GPUs needed.

A: 3{,}200 / 125 = 25.6, so 26 GPUs.
B: 3{,}200 / 2{,}000 = 1.6, so 2 GPUs, fed batches from the shared queue.

This is the chapter’s trade-off in numbers: lowering latency by processing fewer queries at a time underuses hardware and raises the cost per query. Option A meets latency with lots of margin but needs about 13 times the hardware.
Answer: Throughput is 125, 2,000, and 3,200 queries/s. Only A and B meet 30 ms (B at about 26 ms worst case). B serves the traffic on 2 GPUs versus 26 for A, so B is the better choice unless the latency budget tightens.

section: Problem 4: Explaining latency percentiles to a product manager
text:
Problem 4: Explaining latency percentiles to a product manager
Over one minute, a service logged these 20 response latencies in milliseconds, already sorted:
42, 45, 47, 48, 50, 50, 51, 52, 53, 55, 55, 56, 58, 60, 61, 63, 65, 70, 900, 1,200

Compute the mean and the median (p50).
Compute p90 and p95 using two definitions: nearest rank, and linear interpolation (NumPy’s default).
The PM’s dashboard shows “average latency: 154 ms.” What would you tell them?







TipWorked solution





This uses Chapter 1, Latency is a distribution.
1. Mean and median. The values sum to 3,081 ms, so the mean is 3{,}081 / 20 \approx 154 ms. With 20 values, the median is the average of the 10th and 11th: (55 + 55)/2 = 55 ms. Eighteen of the twenty requests took 70 ms or less, so the mean describes almost no actual request.
2. Tail percentiles, two ways.
Nearest rank takes the \lceil q \times n \rceil-th sorted value:

p90: \lceil 0.90 \times 20 \rceil = 18th value, 70 ms.
p95: \lceil 0.95 \times 20 \rceil = 19th value, 900 ms.

Linear interpolation uses position q \times (n-1) in 0-indexed order and interpolates between neighbours:

p90: position 0.90 \times 19 = 17.1, between index 17 (70) and index 18 (900): $70 + 0.1 = $ 153 ms.
p95: position 0.95 \times 19 = 18.05, between index 18 (900) and index 19 (1,200): $900 + 0.05 = $ 915 ms.

p90 is 70 ms under one definition and 153 ms under the other. With only 20 requests, the tail estimate depends on one or two data points.
3. What to tell the PM. The typical request takes about 55 ms. The average is pulled up by two very slow requests (900 and 1,200 ms) that are worth investigating on their own, since they could be a network error or a particular kind of user. The chapter’s Amazon example is a reminder that the slowest requests can come from the most valuable users. Targets should be written as percentiles (for example, “p95 under 100 ms”), measured over enough traffic that the tail is stable. A minute with 20 requests is not enough.
Answer: Mean ≈ 154 ms, p50 = 55 ms. p90 = 70 ms (nearest rank) or 153 ms (interpolated); p95 = 900 or 915 ms. Report percentiles over a larger window, and investigate the two outliers.

section: Problem 5: The ensemble that wins by 0.4 points
text:
Problem 5: The ensemble that wins by 0.4 points
“Your team built a clinical deterioration-risk model. An ensemble of five models reaches an AUC of 0.861 on the validation set; the best single gradient-boosted model reaches 0.857. The ensemble takes about 120 ms per prediction versus 40 ms, and its predictions are harder to explain to clinicians. Which would you ship?”






TipWorked solution





This uses Chapter 1, Stakeholders and requirements and Interpretability.
The chapter’s answer to “which model?” is “it depends on the requirements, and on how strict each one is.” So the strong answer asks the questions that decide it:

Is latency a must-have? If the score is shown live at the bedside, 120 ms may be fine or may not, depending on the screen’s budget. If scores are computed in a nightly batch, latency hardly matters.
Does the 0.004 AUC gain change outcomes? The chapter separates tasks where a small gain is worth a lot (click-through on a large e-commerce site) from tasks where users would not notice. Ask what the gain means at the alert threshold clinicians will actually use: how many more true deteriorations caught, or false alarms avoided, per week. A gain this small on one validation set may also be noise.
What do clinicians need to trust and act on it? Interpretability matters for two reasons in the chapter: users need to understand a decision to trust it and spot bias, and developers need it to debug. If clinicians will not act on an alert they cannot understand, the ensemble’s extra accuracy never reaches patients.
Who maintains it? Five models means five things to retrain, monitor, and debug.

This is the chapter’s ensemble example: ensembles win competitions but are not widely used in production, because they are slower and harder to interpret.
Answer: Default to the single model unless the gain shows up in a meaningful clinical metric at the operating threshold and latency and explainability requirements still allow the ensemble. Make the case with those stakeholder questions, not with AUC alone.

title: Chapter 1 practice: Overview of Machine Learning Systems
text:
Problem 6: 97% accurate overall
“A sepsis screening model is 97% accurate across all patients. One patient subgroup makes up 6% of the population. Can the model still be failing that subgroup? Show how, and say what you would check.”






TipWorked solution





This uses Chapter 1, Fairness.
Yes. Overall accuracy is a weighted average of subgroup accuracies, and a small subgroup barely moves it. Suppose the model is 99% accurate on the other 94% of patients. Then the subgroup accuracy a satisfies

0.94 \times 0.99 + 0.06 \times a = 0.97 ,

so 0.06\,a = 0.97 - 0.9306 = 0.0394 and a \approx 0.66. The model is right on about two-thirds of the subgroup, and the headline number still reads 97%.
The chapter’s version of this point: errors on a minority group have only a small effect on overall metrics, and at scale a model can make those errors about many people at once. It also notes that models “encode the past,” so if the subgroup was under-represented or treated differently in the historical data, the model inherits that.
What to check:

Break every metric down by subgroup, not just accuracy. For a screening task, the subgroup’s miss rate (sensitivity) matters most.
Check representation and labels. How many training examples come from this subgroup, and were their labels recorded the same way?
Check proxies. Features like zip code can encode group membership even when group is not an input.

The same arithmetic explains why accuracy misleads on rare outcomes in general: a model that ignores a small class can still post a high overall number. Chapter 11 covers fairness in depth.
Answer: Yes. 97% overall is consistent with about 66% on a 6% subgroup if everyone else is at 99%. Report metrics per subgroup, focusing on misses, and check the subgroup’s data and proxy features.

section: Problem 7: Performance dropped and nobody changed the code
text:
Problem 7: Performance dropped and nobody changed the code
“Our readmission model’s precision dropped noticeably over the last two months. No one has deployed new code. What could have happened, and what should we have had in place?”






TipWorked solution





This uses Chapter 1, ML systems versus traditional software, Data, and the i.i.d. definition in The five-part test.
In traditional software, unchanged code means unchanged behaviour. An ML system is part code, part data, and part artifacts built from both, so its behaviour can change when only the data changes. Likely causes:

The input distribution moved. New patient mix, a new hospital joining, seasonal illness, or a change in how a lab test is ordered. The model assumed future patients look like training patients (the i.i.d. assumption), and they no longer do.
The relationship changed. A new discharge-follow-up program may have changed who gets readmitted, so the same inputs now lead to different outcomes (concept drift).
An upstream data change. A field renamed, a unit changed, or a default value introduced in the source system. This fails silently: the model still runs.

What should have been in place:

Versioned data and model artifacts, not just code, so we can say exactly what the model was trained on and compare it with what it sees now.
Monitoring of inputs and predictions, so a shift shows up before the outcome labels (readmissions arrive 30 days late) reveal it.
A retraining path, so the model can be updated on recent data.

The book covers monitoring in Chapter 8 and continual learning in Chapter 9.
Answer: The data changed, not the code: input shift, concept drift, or a silent upstream data change. Version data and models as well as code, monitor input and prediction distributions, and have a way to retrain.

title: Chapter 2: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design
text:
Business and ML objectives
Overview. Chapter 1 defined ML systems design as a system approach to MLOps: treating requirements, data, infrastructure, deployment, monitoring, and stakeholders as one whole. This chapter covers the decisions made before any model is trained. Why does the system exist (business objectives, translated into ML objectives)? What must it satisfy (reliability, scalability, maintainability, adaptability)? How does development actually proceed (an iterative cycle, not a line)? And how do we turn a business problem into something a model can learn (choosing the task type and the objective function)? It closes with the debate over whether progress comes from better algorithms or from more data.
Data scientists tend to care about ML objectives: metrics about the model itself, such as accuracy, F1 score, or inference latency. They may spend substantial data, compute, and engineering time raising accuracy from 94% to 94.2%. Why might that effort still get the project cancelled?
Because most companies do not care about ML metrics unless they move a business metric. The book’s view (citing the Friedman doctrine) is that the goal of a project inside a business is to increase profit, either directly (more sales, lower costs) or indirectly (higher customer satisfaction, more time spent on the site). A pattern in short-lived ML projects is a team optimizing ML metrics while their managers, who only see business metrics, cannot tell what the project is doing for the business and shut it down.
Some use cases make the link easy. Every increase in ad click-through rate is ad revenue, and every fraudulent transaction stopped is money saved. That ease of mapping is one reason ad click-through prediction and fraud detection are among the most popular ML use cases.
When the link is not direct, companies build a bridge metric. Netflix measures its recommender by take-rate:
A higher take-rate means more of what the recommender shows actually gets watched. Netflix then checked take-rate against business metrics and found that a higher take-rate went with more total streaming hours and fewer subscription cancellations, which is what makes it a useful proxy.
The effect of a model on the business can be hard to reason about in advance. A more personalized model might make customers happier and spend more, or solve their problems faster and spend less. To settle it, companies run experiments such as A/B tests and pick the model that improves the business metric, even if it is not the model with the better ML metric.
Even experiments are not always enough. The book’s example is a cybersecurity pipeline: a model flags anomalous traffic, if-else rules decide which anomalies are potential threats, security experts review those, and a separate process stops the real ones. When a threat gets through, it may be impossible to tell whether the ML component had anything to do with it.
Finally, be realistic about returns. ML can transform a business, but not overnight. Returns grow with how long a company has been using ML: mature pipelines run more efficiently, iterate faster, need less engineering time, and cost less to run. The book cites a 2020 Algorithmia survey in which companies with models in production for over five years mostly deployed a new model in under 30 days, while most companies just starting took longer than 30 days.

An ML objective is a measurable property of the model (accuracy, F1, latency, loss). An ML project succeeds inside a business only when its ML objectives are tied to the business objectives it is supposed to influence.

title: Chapter 2: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design
text:
Requirements for ML systems
Requirements vary by use case, but the book argues that most ML systems should have four properties.

Reliability

Definition. A system is reliable if it keeps performing the correct function at the desired level of performance even when things go wrong (hardware faults, software faults, human error).

“Correct” is hard to pin down for ML. A system can call model.predict() without error and still return wrong predictions, and without ground truth labels we may not know they are wrong. Traditional software usually fails loudly: a crash, a runtime error, a 404. ML systems can fail silently. If Google Translate mistranslates a sentence into a language you do not read, you have no way to notice. Chapter 8 covers how ML systems fail in production.


Scalability
An ML system can grow in three ways:

Complexity. Last year a logistic regression fit in a 1 GB free-tier cloud instance; this year a 100-million-parameter network needs 16 GB of RAM to serve.
Traffic. From 10,000 prediction requests a day to between 1 and 10 million.
Model count. One model for trending hashtags becomes three when filters for unsafe content and bot posts are added. Enterprise products often grow one model per customer: a startup the author worked with ran 8,000 models for 8,000 customers.


Definition. Scalability is having reasonable ways to handle growth. It covers resource scaling (adding resources when load grows, releasing them when it drops) and artifact management (keeping many models reproducible, monitored, and up to date).

For resource scaling, a system that needs 100 GPUs at peak but 10 most of the time should not keep 100 running. Autoscaling adjusts machine count automatically with usage, but it is hard to get right: Amazon’s autoscaling failed on Prime Day 2018 and the site went down.
For artifact management, one model can be monitored and retrained by hand from a single reproduction script. With a hundred models, monitoring and retraining have to be automated, and you need a systematic way to reproduce any model. The book returns to scaling in Chapter 6 (distributed training), Chapter 7 (model optimization), and Chapter 10 (resource management, experiment tracking and versioning).


Maintainability
Many people work on an ML system: ML engineers, DevOps engineers, and subject matter experts (SMEs), often with different languages and tools. A maintainable system lets each group use the tools they are comfortable with rather than having one group’s tools forced on everyone. Code is documented. Code, data, and artifacts are versioned. Models are reproducible enough that others can build on them after the original authors leave. When something breaks, people can find and fix it together without blaming each other. Chapter 11 covers team structure.


Adaptability

Definition. A system is adaptable if it can discover where performance can be improved and accept updates without interrupting service, so it keeps up with shifting data distributions and changing business requirements.

Recall from Chapter 1 that ML systems are part code and part data, and data changes quickly. Adaptability depends on maintainability: you cannot update quickly what you cannot understand or reproduce. Chapter 8 covers distribution shift and Chapter 9 covers continual learning.

title: Chapter 2: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design
text:
The iterative process
Developing an ML system is iterative and usually never finished: once in production, a system has to be monitored and updated. The book makes this concrete with a story about building a model that decides whether to show an ad for a search query. Condensed:

Choose a metric: impressions (how often an ad is shown).
Collect data, get labels, engineer features, train.
Error analysis shows wrong labels, so relabel and retrain.
Error analysis shows the model always predicts “don’t show,” because 99.99% of the examples are negative. Collect more positive examples and retrain. (This is class imbalance, covered in Chapter 4.)
The model does well on the test set, which is now two months old, but poorly on yesterday’s data. It is stale; retrain on recent data.
Deploy. Then revenue falls: ads are shown, but few are clicked. The metric was wrong. Switch to click-through rate and go back to step 1.

Two of these loops are about the metric, not the model: the system did what it was told, and what it was told did not serve the business.
The book’s generalization of this story is the six-step cycle in Figure 1, drawn from a data scientist’s or ML engineer’s point of view. A platform or DevOps engineer would see the same project differently, with more time spent on infrastructure.

title: Chapter 2: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design
text:
Framing ML problems
Suppose you lead ML engineering at a bank. Your boss hears that a rival bank used ML to handle customer requests twice as fast and asks your team to do the same. Is “speed up customer service” an ML problem?
No. Slow customer service is a business problem.

Definition. An ML problem is defined by three things: the inputs, the outputs, and the objective function that guides learning. Framing a problem means choosing all three.

None of the three is obvious from the request. Investigating, you find the bottleneck is routing each request to the right one of four departments: accounting, inventory, HR, and IT. Now there is an ML problem. The input is the customer request, the output is one of four departments, and the objective is to minimize the difference between the predicted and actual department. This is a classification problem. The rest of this chapter looks at the two choices that most change how hard the problem is: the type of output (the task type) and the objective function. Turning raw inputs into features is Chapter 5.
crumbs: 4  Chapter 2: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design

title: Chapter 2: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design
text:
Types of ML tasks
The model’s output determines the task type. Figure 2 shows the common types.


  
    
  
  Common ML task types

  
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
  

  
  Task type

  
  Regression

  
  Classification

  
  Binary
  
  Multiclass
  
  Multilabel

  
  Low
  cardinality
  
  High
  cardinality

Figure 2. Common task types. Classification splits by the number of classes and by whether an example can carry more than one label (after the book's Figure 2-3).


Classification versus regression

Definition. A classification model assigns each input to one of a set of categories (spam or not spam). A regression model outputs a continuous value (the price of a house).

Either can be reframed as the other.

Regression → classification: bucket house prices (under $100,000; $100,000–$200,000; $200,000–$500,000; and so on) and predict the bucket.
Classification → regression: have the spam model output a value between 0 and 1, then pick a threshold (for example, above 0.5 means spam).

The second reframing is how probabilistic classifiers such as logistic regression already work: the model outputs a score or probability, and a separate decision threshold turns it into a class. The threshold does not have to be 0.5. Where to set it depends on the relative cost of false positives and false negatives, which matters most when one class is rare. The book takes up evaluation metrics in Chapter 6.


Binary versus multiclass classification

Definition. Binary classification has exactly two classes. Multiclass classification has more than two, and each example belongs to exactly one of them.

The book’s binary examples include whether a comment is toxic, whether a lung scan shows signs of cancer, and whether a transaction is fraudulent. Fewer classes generally means an easier problem. Binary problems are easier to work with than multiclass ones: computing F1 or reading a confusion matrix is far more intuitive with two classes.

Definition. A classification task has high cardinality when the number of classes is large, for example thousands of diseases in diagnosis or tens of thousands of products in product classification.

High cardinality is hard first because of data. The author’s rule of thumb is that a model needs at least 100 examples per class to learn that class.






Note



Worked example (the book’s numbers). With 1,000 classes and at least 100 examples each, we need at least 1{,}000 \times 100 = 100{,}000 labeled examples, and that minimum must hold for the rarest class, not just on average. With thousands of classes, some are almost certainly rare, so collecting the minimum for them is the bottleneck.


One remedy is hierarchical classification: one classifier assigns a coarse group, then a second classifier picks a subgroup within it. For products, first classify into electronics, home and kitchen, fashion, or pet supplies; then, for a product classified as fashion, classify into shoes, shirts, jeans, or accessories.


Multiclass versus multilabel classification

Definition. In multilabel classification, an example can belong to more than one class at the same time.

The book’s running example classifies articles into four topics: tech, entertainment, finance, politics. An article can be about both tech and finance. The label encoding shows the difference.



Setting
Label for “entertainment”
Label for “entertainment and finance”




Multiclass (one-hot)
[0, 1, 0, 0]
not allowed


Multilabel (multi-hot)
[0, 1, 0, 0]
[0, 1, 1, 0]



There are two main approaches to a multilabel problem:

Treat it like multiclass, but with multi-hot label vectors.
Turn it into a set of binary problems: one model per topic, each answering “is this article in this topic?”

The author reports that multilabel is the task type companies struggle with most, for two reasons. First, labeling is harder. Annotators may disagree on how many classes an example belongs to (one annotator says two topics, another says one), which is the label multiplicity problem of Chapter 4. Second, turning probabilities into predictions is harder.






Note



Worked example (the book’s numbers). The model outputs [0.45, 0.2, 0.02, 0.33] for [tech, entertainment, finance, politics].

Multiclass: exactly one class is correct, so take the largest: tech (0.45).
Multilabel: the number of correct classes is unknown. Taking the top two gives tech and politics (0.45, 0.33); taking the top three adds entertainment (0.2). Nothing in the output says which is right, so we need an extra rule, such as a per-class threshold or a fixed count.





Multiple ways to frame a problem
The same goal can be framed in ways that make it much easier or harder. The book’s example: predict which app a phone user will open next. Figure 3 compares two framings.


  
    
  
  Two framings of next-app prediction

  
  A. Multiclass classification
  
  User features +
  context (time, location)
  
  
  Model
  
  
  One call: N probabilities, one per app
  Output size tied to N: new app means retraining

  

  
  B. One score per app (the book calls this regression)
  
  User + context + app 0
  
  User + context + app 1
  
  User + context + app ...
  
    
    
    
  
  
  Model
  
  
  N calls: one score in [0, 1] each
  New app is a new input row: no retraining

Figure 3. Framing A ties the model's output layer to the number of apps. Framing B moves the app into the input, so the model scores any app, including new ones (after the book's Figures 2-5 and 2-6).


Framing A (multiclass). Input: the user’s features and the environment’s features (demographics, time, location, previously used apps). Output: a probability distribution over all N apps. One prediction per user per moment, but it is a vector of size N. When a new app is added, we have to retrain the model from scratch, or at least every component whose parameter count depends on N.
Framing B (score each app). Input: the user’s, environment’s, and the app’s features. Output: a single number between 0 and 1, where higher means the user is more likely to open that app. That means N predictions per user per moment, each just a number. A new app needs only its features as a new input row.

The book calls framing B regression because the output is a continuous score. Since the target is whether the user opens the app, it is commonly trained as a binary classifier on (user, context, app) examples with log loss (defined below). Either way, the lesson is the same: moving the item into the input decouples the model from the size of the catalog.

title: Chapter 2: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design
text:
Objective functions
To learn, a model needs an objective function to optimize.

Definition. An objective function is the mathematical function a model optimizes during training. It is also called a loss function, because training usually minimizes the loss caused by wrong predictions. In supervised learning, the loss compares the model’s outputs with the ground-truth labels.

This is a different sense of “objective” from §Business and ML objectives: there, an objective was a goal for the project; here, it is a function the training algorithm minimizes.
Most practitioners use a standard loss rather than designing one:



Task
Common loss




Regression
RMSE (root mean squared error) or MAE (mean absolute error)


Binary classification
Logistic loss (log loss)


Multiclass classification
Cross-entropy



The book gives cross-entropy only as code. The definitions are as follows.

Definition. For a true label distribution p and a predicted distribution q over K classes, the cross-entropy is

H(p, q) = -\sum_{i=1}^{K} p_i \log q_i .

When the label is one-hot with true class k, every term but one vanishes and H(p, q) = -\log q_k.
Log loss is the binary case. For a label y \in \{0, 1\} and predicted probability q that y = 1,

\ell(y, q) = -\big[\, y \log q + (1 - y) \log (1 - q) \,\big].


Cross-entropy only looks at the probability assigned to the true class, and -\log grows sharply as that probability approaches 0. So a confident wrong prediction costs far more than a hesitant one.






Note



Worked example (the book’s numbers). An article’s true topic is politics, so p = [0, 0, 0, 1]. The model outputs q = [0.45, 0.2, 0.02, 0.33].

H(p, q) = -\big(0 \cdot \log 0.45 + 0 \cdot \log 0.2 + 0 \cdot \log 0.02 + 1 \cdot \log 0.33\big) = -\ln 0.33 \approx 1.11 .

Only the 0.33 on the true class counts. Had the model put 0.9 on politics, the loss would be -\ln 0.9 \approx 0.11; had it put 0.02 there, the loss would be -\ln 0.02 \approx 3.91.



Decoupling objectives
Framing gets harder when there are several objectives. The book’s example is ranking posts in a newsfeed. The original goal is to maximize engagement, through three objectives: filter out spam, filter out unsafe content, and rank by engagement (how likely a user is to click).
Optimizing engagement alone turns out to promote extreme posts, which get more engagement. So the goal becomes: maximize engagement while minimizing the spread of extreme views and misinformation. Two objectives are added (filter misinformation, rank by quality), and now two of them conflict. Should an engaging but low-quality post rank high or low?
Each ranking objective becomes a loss. To rank by quality, predict each post’s quality and minimize L_{\text{quality}}, the gap between predicted and true quality. To rank by engagement, predict each post’s clicks and minimize L_{\text{engagement}}, the gap between predicted and actual clicks. There are two ways to combine them (Figure 4).
Option 1: one model, combined loss.


L = \alpha \, L_{\text{quality}} + \beta \, L_{\text{engagement}}


The weights \alpha and \beta set the trade-off, and they can be tuned by trial or more systematically with Pareto (multi-objective) optimization. The cost is that every change to \alpha or \beta means retraining, for example when quality rises but engagement falls and we want to shift weight toward engagement.
Option 2: one model per objective, combined scores. Train a quality model that minimizes L_{\text{quality}} and outputs a quality score, and an engagement model that minimizes L_{\text{engagement}} and outputs predicted clicks. Rank posts by


\text{score} = \alpha \cdot \text{quality score} + \beta \cdot \text{engagement score}


Now \alpha and \beta can change without retraining anything.


  
    
  
  Combined loss vs decoupled models

  
  Option 1: one model
  
  Posts
  
  
  One model trained on
  α · quality loss + β · engagement loss
  
  
  Ranking
  Change α or β: retrain

  Change α or β: no retraining

Figure 4. Folding both objectives into one loss fixes the trade-off at training time. Separate models move the trade-off to ranking time.

The book’s general advice: when there are multiple objectives, decouple them first. Two reasons:

Tuning without retraining. The trade-off between objectives can be adjusted at ranking time.
Separate maintenance schedules. Spam tactics change much faster than how people judge post quality, so the spam filter needs updating far more often than the quality ranker.

This resolves the conflict from Chapter 1’s restaurant app: one model for what users will order, one for what earns the most, and a tunable combination of the two.

title: Chapter 2: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design
text:
Mind versus data
Is progress in ML driven by better algorithms (the “mind” side, including inductive biases and clever architectures) or by more data and the computation that comes with it? In principle we can pursue both, but time spent on one is usually taken from the other.



Mind over data
Data over mind




Judea Pearl: “Data is profoundly dumb.” In 2020 he predicted that data-centric ML practitioners would be outdated within 3–5 years.
Richard Sutton, “The Bitter Lesson”: general methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective, by a large margin.


Christopher Manning (milder): huge compute and data with a simple learning algorithm make very bad learners; structure lets systems learn more from less data.
Peter Norvig, on Google Search: “We don’t have better algorithms. We just have more data.”



Monica Rogati’s “data science hierarchy of needs” makes the data side concrete: data collection and infrastructure sit at the base of a pyramid with ML near the top, so without good data (quality and quantity) there is no data science.
The book frames the debate precisely: nobody doubts that finite data is necessary; the question is whether it is sufficient. With infinite data we might simply look up the answer, but a lot of data is not infinite data.
For now, the trend favors data. Language-model datasets grew from 0.8 billion tokens (the One Billion Word Benchmark, 2013) to 10 billion (GPT-2, 2019) to 500 billion (GPT-3, 2020). But more data is not automatically better. More data of lower quality, such as outdated data or incorrectly labeled data, can hurt performance. That is the motivation for the data chapters that follow.

title: Chapter 2: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design
text:
Summary






Note



Key takeaways from Chapter 2 (and what an interviewer is usually checking):

Start from the business metric. ML metrics matter only if they move a business metric. Bridge metrics (take-rate) and A/B tests connect the two, and the model with the better business result wins even if its ML metric is worse.
Four requirements: reliability, scalability, maintainability, adaptability. ML fails silently; scaling covers complexity, traffic, and model count, plus artifact management; adaptability depends on maintainability.
Development is a cycle. Scoping, data, modeling, deployment, monitoring, business analysis, then back to scoping. Real iterations are often caused by the wrong metric or the wrong data rather than the wrong model.
Framing means choosing inputs, outputs, and the objective function. Classification and regression convert into each other; a probability plus a threshold is a classifier, and the threshold is a choice.
Know the task types and their difficulties. Binary is easiest; high cardinality needs data for rare classes (hierarchical classification helps); multilabel is hard to label and hard to decode.
Framing changes difficulty. Putting the item into the input (one score per app) avoids retraining whenever the catalog changes.
Know the standard losses. RMSE/MAE for regression, log loss for binary, cross-entropy for multiclass; with one-hot labels, cross-entropy is -\log of the probability on the true class.
Decouple multiple objectives. Separate models plus a weighted score let you retune trade-offs without retraining and maintain each model on its own schedule.
Data matters, but quality matters too. More low-quality data can make a model worse.



Next chapter: Chapter 3, Data Engineering Fundamentals, covers data sources, data formats, data models, storage engines for transactional and analytical processing, how data passes between processes, and batch versus stream processing.

title: Chapter 2 practice: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design
text:
Problem 1: The AUC went up and nothing else did
Overview. These are interview-style questions on Chapter 2. Answer each one out loud before opening the worked solution. The scenarios and numbers are invented for practice. Each solution says which chapter section it draws on, walks through the reasoning, and ends with a short answer you could give.
“Our team built a model that ranks patients by how likely they are to be eligible for a clinical trial, so recruiters call the most promising ones first. We raised the model’s AUC from 0.78 to 0.84 over a quarter. Enrollment didn’t change. Leadership wants to cancel the project. What went wrong, and what would you do now?”
crumbs: 5  Chapter 2 practice: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design

title: Chapter 2 practice: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design
text:
TipWorked solution





This uses Chapter 2, Business and ML objectives.
The team optimized an ML objective (AUC) without checking that it moves the business objective (enrollment). That is the chapter’s pattern for short-lived projects: data scientists improve ML metrics, managers see no business result, the project is cancelled.
Possible reasons the gain did not reach enrollment:

The bottleneck is elsewhere. If recruiters already reach everyone on the list, or trial sites cannot take more patients, a better ranking changes nothing.
The gain is where it does not matter. AUC summarizes the whole ranking. Recruiters only call the top of the list, and the improvement may be in the part they never reach.
Eligibility is not enrollment. Eligible patients may still decline. The model predicts the first step, and the business needs the last.

What to do:

Define a bridge metric, the way Netflix uses take-rate, that sits between the model and the business outcome. For example: the fraction of patients called from the top of the list who end up enrolling.
Run an A/B test. Let some recruiters work from the new ranking and some from the old (or from the current manual process), and compare enrollment. The chapter’s rule is to choose the model that improves the business metric, whether or not its ML metric is better.
Scope the next iteration from the result. That is step 6 of the iterative cycle (business analysis) feeding back into step 1.

Answer: AUC was never tied to enrollment. Find where the real bottleneck is, define a metric that links the ranking to enrollment, and A/B test the model against the current process before investing more in AUC.

title: Chapter 2 practice: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design
section: Problem 2: The unit change nobody announced
text:
Problem 2: The unit change nobody announced
“A hospital’s lab system changed how it reports blood glucose, from mg/dL to mmol/L, without telling the ML team. Our risk model, which uses glucose as an input, kept running with no errors for three weeks. Which system requirement does this test, and how would you have caught it?”






TipWorked solution





This uses Chapter 2, Reliability and Adaptability.
This is the chapter’s silent failure case, so the requirement is reliability. Traditional software tends to fail loudly with a crash or an error. Here predict() ran fine on every request, but glucose values were now roughly 18 times smaller (1 mmol/L of glucose is about 18 mg/dL), so the model saw every patient as having very low glucose. Nothing errored, so nothing alerted.
We cannot wait for ground truth to catch this: outcome labels may arrive weeks later, and by then patients have been mis-scored. Checks that do not need labels:

Input monitoring. Track each feature’s distribution. A sudden drop in the median of a key feature (for glucose, by a factor of about 18) is easy to detect.
Schema and range checks at the input boundary. A glucose value of 5 is plausible in mmol/L but implausible in mg/dL.
Prediction monitoring. A sudden shift in the share of high-risk predictions is a signal even when no single input looks wrong.

Recovering also tests adaptability (can we fix the input path and update without stopping service?) and maintainability (do data owners and ML engineers have a shared contract and a way to work through a problem without blame?). Chapter 8 covers monitoring in detail.
Answer: Reliability, because this is a silent failure. Catch it without labels by monitoring input distributions, validating ranges and units at ingestion, and watching the distribution of predictions.

title: Chapter 2 practice: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design
section: Problem 3: “Use AI to reduce clinic no-shows”
text:
Problem 3: “Use AI to reduce clinic no-shows”
“Our outpatient clinics lose a lot of capacity to patients who miss appointments. Leadership asks you to ‘use AI to reduce no-shows.’ Turn this into an ML problem, and tell me how you would know it worked.”






TipWorked solution





This uses Chapter 2, Framing ML problems, Classification versus regression, and Objective functions.
“Reduce no-shows” is a business problem, like the chapter’s “speed up customer service.” An ML problem needs inputs, outputs, and an objective function. First ask what action the prediction will drive, because that decides what to predict. Common actions are an extra reminder call or controlled overbooking of a slot.
A framing that supports those actions:

Input: one scheduled appointment, described by features known at booking or reminder time, such as lead time between booking and visit, the patient’s past attendance, appointment type, and day and time.
Output: the probability that this appointment will be a no-show. That is binary classification, with a probability output.
Objective function: log loss, the standard loss for binary classification.
Decision: a threshold on the probability decides who gets the extra call. It should be set from the cost of a call versus the cost of an empty slot, not left at 0.5.

How to know it worked: the business metric is the no-show rate (or the share of clinic capacity used), not AUC. Run an A/B test: patients flagged by the model get the intervention, and a comparable group gets the current process.
One more point from Chapter 1: check features for fairness. Distance from the clinic or zip code can act as a proxy for income, and “overbook the patients predicted to miss” can systematically disadvantage some groups.
Answer: Predict, per appointment, the probability of a no-show (binary classification, log loss), threshold it to trigger a reminder or overbooking, and judge it by an A/B test on the no-show rate, with a fairness check on proxy features.

Problem 4: Choosing a threshold for a rare, serious event
A model scores 10 patients for risk of a serious adverse reaction. Two of them (A and B) actually had the reaction.

At a threshold of 0.5, count the true positives, false positives, and false negatives. Do the same at 0.3.
Compute the accuracy at each threshold, and the accuracy of a model that always predicts “no reaction.”
Which threshold would you argue for, and why?







TipWorked solution





This uses Chapter 2, Classification versus regression.
The chapter frames a classifier as a model that outputs a score between 0 and 1 plus a threshold that turns the score into a class. The threshold is a choice.
1. Counts.

Threshold 0.5: flagged are A (0.62) and C (0.55). A had the reaction, C did not. TP = 1, FP = 1, FN = 1 (B, at 0.38, is missed), TN = 7.
Threshold 0.3: flagged are A, C, D, B, and E. TP = 2, FP = 3, FN = 0, TN = 5.

2. Accuracy.

At 0.5: (1 + 7)/10 = 80\%.
At 0.3: (2 + 5)/10 = 70\%.
Always “no reaction”: 8 of 10 correct, 80%.

By accuracy, the 0.5 threshold looks better than 0.3, and it ties a model that never flags anyone. That is why accuracy misleads when one class is rare: the large class dominates the count.
3. The argument. For a serious reaction, a missed case (FN) costs far more than an extra check on a patient who would have been fine (FP). At 0.3 we catch both reactions at the cost of two more false alarms. Whether that is right depends on what a flag triggers: if it means extra monitoring, false alarms are cheap and 0.3 or lower is reasonable; if it means withholding a useful drug, false alarms are expensive.
Choosing an evaluation metric that reflects those costs (for example, recall at a fixed precision) is covered in Chapter 6, and handling class imbalance in Chapter 4.
Answer: At 0.5, TP 1, FP 1, FN 1 (80% accuracy); at 0.3, TP 2, FP 3, FN 0 (70%); always-negative is 80%. Argue for the lower threshold if missing a reaction is worse than a false alarm, and say that accuracy is the wrong yardstick here.

section: Problem 5: Cross-entropy and log loss by hand
text:
Problem 5: Cross-entropy and log loss by hand
A model grades adverse-event severity into three classes: [none, mild, severe]. For a patient whose true severity is severe, compute the cross-entropy loss for each of these predicted distributions:


q = [0.05, 0.10, 0.85]


q = [0.30, 0.30, 0.40]


q = [0.80, 0.15, 0.05]


Then, for a binary model that predicts a 0.2 probability of an event, compute the log loss when the event did happen (y = 1) and when it did not (y = 0). Use natural logarithms.






TipWorked solution





This uses Chapter 2, Objective functions.
The true label is one-hot: p = [0, 0, 1]. Cross-entropy is H(p, q) = -\sum_i p_i \log q_i, and with a one-hot label only the true class’s term survives, so H = -\log q_{\text{severe}}.


-\ln 0.85 \approx 0.16. Confident and correct: small loss.


-\ln 0.40 \approx 0.92. Unsure, but leaning correct: moderate loss.


-\ln 0.05 \approx 3.00. Confident and wrong: large loss.


The probabilities on “none” and “mild” do not enter the loss directly. They matter only by taking probability away from the true class. Because -\log grows sharply near 0, (c) costs almost 20 times as much as (a).
For the binary case, log loss is \ell(y, q) = -[\,y \log q + (1-y)\log(1-q)\,] with q = 0.2:

y = 1: -\ln 0.2 \approx 1.61. The event happened and the model said 20%.
y = 0: -\ln 0.8 \approx 0.22. No event, and the model leaned that way.

Answer: (a) ≈ 0.16, (b) ≈ 0.92, (c) ≈ 3.00. Log loss ≈ 1.61 when y = 1 and ≈ 0.22 when y = 0.

title: Chapter 2 practice: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design
section: Problem 6: Patients with more than one diagnosis
text:
Problem 6: Patients with more than one diagnosis
“We want a model that reads a discharge summary and outputs the patient’s diagnoses. A patient can have several at once. How would you frame this, and what goes wrong if we treat it as ordinary multiclass? Later the team wants to predict specific diagnosis codes, of which there are thousands. What changes?”
For a concrete case, suppose for one summary the model outputs these probabilities for four conditions: diabetes 0.81, hypertension 0.64, chronic kidney disease 0.38, asthma 0.06.






TipWorked solution





This uses Chapter 2, Multiclass versus multilabel classification and Binary versus multiclass classification.
Framing. Each patient can have several diagnoses, so this is multilabel classification. For [diabetes, hypertension, CKD, asthma], a patient with diabetes and hypertension has the multi-hot label [1, 1, 0, 0]. Multiclass would force a one-hot label and could record only one diagnosis.
The two approaches from the chapter:

One model with a multi-hot output (one probability per condition, not forced to sum to 1).
One binary model per condition (“does this patient have diabetes?”).

Why multiclass breaks, using the example. Multiclass picks the single top class: diabetes. That silently drops hypertension, which at 0.64 is also likely. Multilabel needs a decoding rule instead:

A threshold of 0.5 per condition gives diabetes and hypertension.
“Take the top 3” adds CKD at 0.38.

Nothing in the output says which is right. That is the chapter’s second reason multilabel is hard. The first is labeling: coders may disagree on how many diagnoses a summary supports (the label multiplicity problem of Chapter 4).
Thousands of codes. Now the task also has high cardinality. With the chapter’s rule of thumb of at least 100 examples per class, 5,000 codes would need at least 500,000 labeled examples, with at least 100 for each rare code, which many rare codes will not have. A common remedy is hierarchical classification: diagnosis codes are already organized into chapters and blocks, so predict the broad group first and the specific code within it second.
Answer: Multilabel, with multi-hot labels, using one multi-output model or one binary model per condition, and a decoding rule such as per-class thresholds (here giving diabetes and hypertension). At thousands of codes, expect too few examples for rare codes, and consider predicting through the code hierarchy.
